title: The ENTIRE History of the Aztec Empire in 10 Minutes
youtube_title: The ENTIRE History of the Aztec Empire in 10 Minutes (1325–1521)
description:
From a swampy island in a lake to one of the biggest cities on Earth, this is the whole story of the Aztec Empire from 1325 to 1521 in about ten minutes: the eagle legend, the Triple Alliance, the floating city of Tenochtitlan, chinampa farms, cacao-bean money, Moctezuma's chocolate, Cortés and his Indigenous allies, smallpox, and the fall of the city. Every fact is checked.

Chapters are added automatically.

#history #aztecs #aztecempire #tenochtitlan #animatedhistory

beats.say: November 1519. A few hundred Spanish soldiers march along a stone road built straight across a lake.
At the end of it floats a city of white towers, temples and canals, with thousands of canoes.
Am I dreaming? Somebody pinch me. Is this real?
If you're dreaming, then I'm having the same dream.
Decades later, Bernal Díaz wrote: And some of our soldiers even asked whether the things that we saw were not a dream.

show.text: And some of our soldiers even asked whether the things that we saw were not a dream.
show.who: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, The True History of the Conquest of New Spain (trans. A. P. Maudslay)

beats.say: Less than two years later, that city would lie in ruins.
So who built a city in the middle of a lake, and how did it fall so fast? Let's start at the beginning.

show.text: The ENTIRE History of the Aztec Empire in 10 Minutes
show.sub: From a swamp island to a superpower, 1325 to 1521

beats.say: In the 1200s, a people called the Mexica walked into the Valley of Mexico, a high valley full of lakes.
They were late. All the good land was already taken by older, richer cities.
So the Mexica worked as hired soldiers for their neighbors, and kept getting kicked out.
Around 1325, they settled on a swampy island in Lake Texcoco, a big, shallow lake.
Their legend says their god, Huitzilopochtli, told them to look for a sign: an eagle on a cactus, eating a snake.
There it is! Eagle, cactus, snake. This is the spot!
In a swamp? The god couldn't pick somewhere with dry floors?
Nobody knows if anyone really saw that eagle. But the Mexica built their city there and called it Tenochtitlan.
Remember that eagle. It's still on a famous flag today, and we'll come back to it.
For about a hundred years, Tenochtitlan was a small fish. It paid tribute, a kind of tax, to a stronger city called Azcapotzalco.
Then a new Mexica ruler, Itzcoatl, made a deal with two neighbors, the cities of Texcoco and Tlacopan.
So. You hate paying Azcapotzalco?
I hate paying Azcapotzalco. Let's beat them, and then they can pay us.
In 1428, the three cities beat Azcapotzalco together. Historians call them the Triple Alliance. Most of us call it the Aztec Empire.
Fun fact: they never called themselves Aztecs. They were the Mexica. The word Aztec caught on centuries later, through European writers like Alexander von Humboldt.
The empire grew by conquest. Beaten cities kept their rulers, but sent tribute: cotton cloth, feathers, food and cacao beans.
Pictures of those tribute lists survive in a book made for the Spanish, called the Codex Mendoza.

show.title: Building a City on a Lake

beats.say: Now the fun part. How do you build a giant city on a lake?
First, causeways: long raised roads across the water, with bridges you could pull up in a war.
Then canals everywhere. Canoes carried people and goods, like a city of floating taxis.
Part of the lake was salty, so a long dike, a wall across the lake, kept the salty water out. Accounts credit Nezahualcoyotl, the poet king of Texcoco.
Fresh drinking water came in through an aqueduct, a stone pipe from the springs on Chapultepec hill.
For food, they built chinampas: little farm islands made of lake mud and plants, held in place by willow trees.
The mud was so rich that farmers could grow several crops a year, right in the middle of a lake.
In the center stood the Great Temple, a huge pyramid with two shrines on top.
It was also where the Aztecs' darkest custom happened. Priests sacrificed war captives there, believing the gods needed it to keep the sun moving.
Historians argue about how many died. The custom made the empire feared, and hated, by many of its neighbors.
By 1500, Tenochtitlan was huge. Estimates vary a lot, but many historians say about two hundred thousand people.

show.label: Tenochtitlan, about 1500
show.sub: people, by many estimates (guesses range from under 100,000 to 300,000)

beats.say: That's bigger than any city in Spain. Seville had maybe fifty thousand. Only a few giants, like Paris and Naples, were in the same league.
In 1502, a new emperor took the throne: Moctezuma the Second.
His capital had a twin city, Tlatelolco, with a giant market. Cortés later claimed sixty thousand people shopped there every day.
There were no coins. People mostly swapped goods, but for small things they paid with cacao beans, the beans chocolate is made from.
A price list from 1545, soon after the Spanish arrived, says one bean bought a big tomato, and a turkey cost a hundred beans.

show.label: One cacao bean bought
show.sub: a turkey hen cost 100 beans (Tlaxcala price list, 1545)

beats.say: And where there's money, there's fake money.
Hmm. This bean feels very light.
That's not fake. That's a diet bean.
Spanish-era writers say crooks emptied real beans and stuffed them with dirt, or shaped fakes out of wax and dough.
Kids went to school, too. Spanish-era sources say every boy, rich or poor, went to one: special schools for nobles' sons, and neighborhood schools for everyone else.
That was unusual back then. In most of the world, poor kids rarely saw a classroom.
Moctezuma lived in style. The Spanish wrote that he kept a zoo with jaguars, eagles and snakes, and hundreds of keepers.
And he loved chocolate. Back then it was a bitter, foamy drink, with no sugar at all.
Bernal Díaz wrote that at one meal, servants brought him about fifty big jugs of it, all frothed up.
Meanwhile, across the ocean, in 1492, Christopher Columbus had sailed west from Spain.
Spain soon grabbed islands in the Caribbean, like Cuba, and a lot of ambitious young Spaniards moved there.
One of them was Hernán Cortés, from Medellín, a small town in Spain.
In 1519 he sailed from Cuba to Mexico with eleven ships and about five hundred Spanish soldiers.
On the way he gained an interpreter, Malintzin. She had been handed to the Spanish as a captive, spoke the Aztec language, and quickly learned Spanish.
Sink the ships.
Sink our only ride home? Great plan, boss.
The famous story says he burned them. Actually, he had them stripped and sunk, so nobody could sail back to Cuba.
Then he marched inland. The Tlaxcalans, longtime enemies of the Aztecs, fought him first, then joined him.
Many cities hated paying Aztec tribute, and saw the Spanish as a useful weapon.
On the eighth of November 1519, Moctezuma welcomed Cortés into Tenochtitlan as a guest, with gifts of gold.
About a week later, Cortés repaid him by taking him prisoner in his own city.
Cortés also sent Aztec treasures to his king, Charles the Fifth. In 1520 they were shown in Brussels.
The German artist Albrecht Dürer saw them and wrote: All the days of my life I have seen nothing that rejoiced my heart so much as these things.

show.text: All the days of my life I have seen nothing that rejoiced my heart so much as these things.

beats.say: In 1520, everything fell apart.
Cortés left the city to fight a rival Spanish force on the coast, and put his captain, Pedro de Alvarado, in charge.
During a religious festival at the Great Temple, Alvarado's men attacked the unarmed crowd and killed many people.
The city rose up. Soon Moctezuma was dead. Spanish and Aztec accounts disagree about who killed him.
On the night of the thirtieth of June, the Spanish tried to slip out along a causeway. Hundreds died, some weighed down, accounts say, by the gold they carried.
Then came something deadlier than any army: smallpox.
The disease came with the Europeans. People in the Americas had never met it, so their bodies had no defense.
It swept through Tenochtitlan in the fall of 1520. Historians estimate it killed between a quarter and half of the people of central Mexico.

show.label: Smallpox in central Mexico, 1520
show.sub: people may have died, historians estimate

beats.say: The new emperor, Cuitláhuac, Moctezuma's brother, died of it after only about eighty days on the throne.
Cortés regrouped with his allies in Tlaxcala, then came back in 1521 with thirteen small warships built to fight on the lake.
But most of the army wasn't Spanish. Tens of thousands of Indigenous warriors, from Tlaxcala and other cities, did most of the fighting.
The Spanish themselves had only about a thousand soldiers.

show.label: At the final siege
show.sub: Spanish soldiers, beside tens of thousands of Indigenous allies

beats.say: They cut off the causeways and the fresh water. Inside the city, food and water ran out.
The young new emperor, Cuauhtémoc, held out for nearly three months.
On the thirteenth of August 1521, he was captured in a canoe on the lake, and Tenochtitlan fell.
The Spanish tore the city down and built their own capital right on top: Mexico City.
Over the centuries, the lake was drained. But the city still sits on the soft old lake bed, and some parts sink more than twenty centimeters a year.
In 1978, electricity workers digging in the city center hit a giant carved stone.
It led archaeologists to the ruins of the Great Temple, right in the middle of the modern city.
More than a million Mexicans still speak Nahuatl, the Aztec language. And so do you, a little: chocolate, tomato, avocado and chili all come from it.
And that eagle on a cactus, eating a snake? It's right in the middle of Mexico's flag today.

show.label: MEXICO
show.sub: Today's flag, with the eagle from the founding legend

beats.say: So that's the Aztecs: latecomers on a swampy island who built one of the biggest cities on Earth, in less than two hundred years.
